articles.text: Stop wasting taxpayers’ money Editor: No matter our political leanings, here’s something we can all agree on: Don’t waste taxpayer dollars. Neighbors around Nova and Magnolia are asking the City not to spend money on a project we do not want. In 2019, the City of Piedmont installed its first use of plastic bollards to calm traffic at the intersection of Nova and Magnolia. The bollards compromised the neighborhood aesthetic, and in letters and testimony at council meetings, neighbors urged the City to take a different approach. We were told the bollards were only temporary, simply a trial design for a landscaped solution. This eyesore was supposed to enhance safety but has not. The bollards have created confusion and posed their own safety risks. Neighbors have asked the City repeatedly to remove the bollards ASAP, but, even in the face of a petition signed by 120 residents, the bollards are still there. Now the City is proposing to install black and orange asphalt bumpers at a cost of $50,000 in lieu of the bollards. But these, too, are ugly and pose safety risks. Neighbors have done everything the City asked in order to get a landscaped solution. For example, we were told to go to the CIP, and nothing occurred. We were told to raise funds which we did but were rebuffed. Now we have some simple requests to the City: 1. Remove the bollards 2. Do not spend $50,000 of taxpayer money to foist on residents raised eyesore markers that are inappropriate to the neighborhood. Many of us are longtime residents and all of us are taxpayers. This intersection, which abuts a main Piedmont artery, deserves more than a slipshod solution. If we have to raise money, we need a good list of options and how much money each would cost. Perhaps nothing further is even needed. This is all common sense. Spending $50,000 would be folly. Let’s hope a majority of the City Council agrees. –Joy Koletsky Jacobs

articles.text: A weekend walk-in clinic offering monkeypox vaccinations opened at San Francisco General Hospital on Saturday, August 14. A quarter of the state’s monkeypox cases are in San Francisco. The federal government announced its national monkeypox vaccine strategy on June 28. Multiple federal agencies coordinated to implement a plan to inoculate at-risk individuals with a limited supply of vaccines. Long lines were reported at monkeypox vaccine pop-up clinics throughout the state when the Jynneos vaccine first became available. The Jynneos monkeypox vaccine is administered in two doses similar to the Moderna and Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine. San Francisco resident Joe Haley said he waited in line over three hours to receive his first dose at San Francisco General Hospital on August 1. Haley arrived at 5:30 a.m. as a walk-in patient and was given a patient information sheet to fill out, and then a number for inoculation: #149. “I showed up before the clinic opened and was expecting a lot of people. The [hospital] staff were efficient despite the long line and wait time,” Haley said. The patient information sheet required that each walk-in patient state their name, address and phone number, as well as sexual identity and sexual orientation. The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said in a press release on May 18 that “anyone can spread monkeypox regardless of sexual orientation,” while also noting that early case tracking suggests “gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men make up a high number of cases.” Haley, who identifies as gay, said he sought out the vaccine after hearing of the first confirmed case of the virus in San Francisco. “The symptoms [associated with the virus] sound and look excruciating. There is definitely a sense of alarm in the gay community,” he said. Haley lives in the Castro District of San Francisco. San Francisco General Hospital is one of the closest pop-up clinics offering the Jynneos monkeypox vaccine. At the time of his first inoculation on August 1, Haley was not given a date to return for his second dose. The vaccine series is administered in the upper arm at least four weeks apart. According to the CDC, people who receive the vaccine have minor reactions such as pain, redness, and swelling at the injection site. Rare reactions such as nausea, chills, and fever have been reported. Vaccine supply is limited. San Francisco General Hospital received over 10,000 doses from the federal supply last week, allowing it to reopen and inoculate individuals seeking vaccinations. The vaccine is free and no health insurance is required. In San Francisco, gay, bisexual, and men who have sex with men; sex workers of any sexual orientation; persons who have been in close contact with someone with a suspected or confirmed case of the virus; and clinicians who have had a high-risk occupational exposure are eligible to receive the Jynneos vaccine. The San Francisco Department of Public Health (SFDPH) explained in a statement that it will prioritize first dose of Jynneos vaccine “to as many at-risk people as possible and will defer second dose appointments until sufficient supply is received.” The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) has created a screening worksheet and urges all individuals with symptoms of Monkeypox to complete the worksheet, which requires the patient to send photos of rashes and collect specimens. The form is available at https://acphd-web-media.s3-uswest-2.amazonaws.com/media/ communicable-disease/monkeypox/docs/monkeypox-screening-form-2022.07.10.pdf.

articles.text: Editor: Hundreds of pages of technical analyses as well as scores of hours of public testimony regarding housing for low-income families in Piedmont boil down to a simple question: do we want to live in a segregated city in which low-income families reside, as a matter of public policy, in a concentrated enclave socially and physically isolated from the remainder of the community? Comments at public hearings suggest that some Piedmonters would answer “yes.” They suggest locating 100 or more low-income families in Blair Park – noisier, more hazardous, more distant from schools, and more physically isolated than any site the city’s professional staff recommended the City Council consider. Fifty years of research into the costs and benefits of subsidized housing tells us, however, that concentrating low-income families in an area functionally separate from the remainder of the community is the worst choice a city can make. Indeed, federal, state, and local, including Piedmont, policy is to avoid such concentration. Ignoring those policies and concentrating 100 or more low-income families in Blair Park would create a place that all Piedmonters will know as the “other side of tracks.” A stigmatized place that impedes rather than fosters participation in the larger community. And, yes, research also suggests that adding low-income housing to high income communities reduces property values, at least temporarily. But those effects are smaller and shorter in duration when cities “scatter” rather than segregate such housing. The State’s requirement that we accommodate 220 low and very low-income families means we cannot preserve all Piedmont neighborhoods as we now know them. We can, however, choose whether Piedmont will welcome or impede the participation of these families in the social and civic life of our community. This choice will profoundly influence how Piedmont families, regardless of income, come to view, and live with, each other. It will also affect how others in our region view us now and into the indefinite future. Do you prefer a segregated Piedmont to one that keeps open the possibility of creating a community, however imperfect, of which we can all be proud? If not, please let the City Council know your preferences in advance of the August 18 City Council meeting. –Ralph Catalano For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: The City of Piedmont will be piloting a self-haul compost program that offers free compost for Piedmont residents to pick up on specific days, as weather and availability allow. This pilot program is different than the recent free compost giveaway events, in that the compost will be available to residents to self-haul every Friday during the summer months. The compost is first-come, first-served, and City staff cannot guarantee or confirm availability of compost. To pick up compost, you should bring your own shovel, container, and gloves to load the materials yourself. Pick-up trucks must tarp their loads. A quarter of the state’s monkeypox cases are in San Francisco. The federal government announced its national monkeypox vaccine strategy on June 28. Multiple federal agencies coordinated to implement a plan to inoculate at-risk individuals with a limited supply of vaccines. By Ralph Catalano Editor: Hundreds of pages of technical analyses as well as scores of hours of public testimony regarding housing for low-income families in Piedmont boil down to a simple question: do we want to live in a segregated city in which low-income families reside, as a matter of public policy, in a concentrated enclave socially and physically isolated from the remainder of the community? Comments at public hearings suggest that some Piedmonters would answer “yes.” They suggest locating 100 or more low-income families in Blair Park – noisier, more hazardous, more distant from schools, and more physically isolated than any site the city’s professional staff recommended the City Council consider. Fifty years of research into the costs and benefits of subsidized housing tells us, however, that concentrating low-income families in an area functionally separate from the remainder of the community is the worst choice a city can make. Indeed, federal, state, and local, including Piedmont, policy is to avoid such concentration. Ignoring those policies and concentrating 100 or more low-income families in Blair Park would create a place that all Piedmonters will know as the “other side of tracks.” A stigmatized place that impedes rather than fosters participation in the larger community. And, yes, research also suggests that adding low-income housing to high income communities reduces property values, at least temporarily. But those effects are smaller and shorter in duration when cities “scatter” rather than segregate such housing. The State’s requirement that we accommodate 220 low and very low-income families means we cannot preserve all Piedmont neighborhoods as we now know them. We can, however, choose whether Piedmont will welcome or impede the participation of these families in the social and civic life of our community. This choice will profoundly influence how Piedmont families, regardless of income, come to view, and live with, each other. It will also affect how others in our region view us now and into the indefinite future. Do you prefer a segregated Piedmont to one that keeps open the possibility of creating a community, however imperfect, of which we can all be proud? If not, please let the City Council know your preferences in advance of the August 18 City Council meeting. –Ralph Catalano Collecting photos for Where in the World For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: Photo by Brian Mahany The Yulan Magnolia (magnolia denudate) in the forecourt at Piedmont Community Hall, is recognized in the city’s Heritage Tree program and will be included in the city’s tree inventory. Piedmont Public Works is conducting a citywide tree inventory of its urban forest, a project that will take two to three months. The City announced on August 10 that Davey Resource Group [DRG] will canvass and record the thousands of public trees in Piedmont. “During the inventory, DRG’s experienced, qualified urban foresters locate trees, planting sites, and stumps along maintained street right-of-ways and in public parks and properties,” said Parks and Projects Manager Nancy Kent. “The arborists will evaluate those trees and record the data specified by the city.” DRG’s staff will identify the species, location, diameter, and health of over 8,000 trees in the coming weeks. They began collecting data on August 9. “Residents will see arborists walking our streets and parks with their iPads reviewing the trees of our urban forest,” Kent said. “They will be identifiable by their safety vest and hard hats and will carry a badge.” Public Works Supervisor Nik Millosovich explained the importance of the tree inventory. “The city has not done a tree inventory since the mid-to-late 1980’s, and the city’s tree inventory has changed quite a bit in that time,” he said. Parks and public areas are maintained by the Public Works Department; the Park Commission, Piedmont Beautification Foundation and Piedmont Garden Club contribute to the maintenance of the city’s diverse landscape. Millosovich confirmed that the majority of the city’s mature trees are Liquidambar and London Plane. Also included in the city’s public tree stock are Maples, Highland Poplars, Coast Redwoods, and European White Birches.

articles.text: The city of Piedmont anticipates construction on the Piedmont Community Pool to begin in late November or early December this year. Bid documents will be distributed to pre-qualified contractors this month and opening bids will begin in early October. “This marks an important milestone in the process of bringing a new community pool to Piedmont. We are ready to solicit bids for construction,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said to the City Council on August 16. The project defines a base bid that includes: a single-story pool building with an office, lobby, locker rooms, two gender neutral changing rooms and rooftop pavilion; 27-meter x 25-yard competition pool with diving well; 3,177 square foot Activity Pool with zero beach entry and three 25-yard lap lanes; an all-electric powered aquatic center, including building, site and pool systems; and right-of way improvements. “Due to the unique nature of the Community Pool Project, council members authorized city staff to prepare a pre-qualification request [RFQ] at the May 16 meeting to ensure that only contractors fully capable of successfully constructing the project would be invited to submit bid proposals,” Lillevand said. The RFQ was issued on June 1, and six bid proposals were received by the July 1 deadline. After a detailed review, two firms, Lathrop Construction Associates and S.J. Amoroso Construction Co., were pre-qualified to bid on the City’s Community Pool Project, Lillevand explained. The bid documents specify that the estimated time to complete the project is 335 working days, which keeps the project on track for opening in the summer of 2024. Photo courtesy of ELS Architecture and Urban Design Construction on the Piedmont Community Pool is expected to begin this winter, according to city staff.

articles.text: The following letter was sent on August 14 to Piedmont City Council. Editor: We are writing to you in your official capacities as mayor and city council of Piedmont because the recent curb work at the intersection of Manor Drive and Holly Place is unsafe and unsightly. The neighborhood was afforded absolutely no opportunity to weigh in on the design before it was adopted. In short, we went from a typical Piedmont curb allowing pedestrians to travel freely through the intersection to an ugly sunken maze of tripping hazards. Two days ago, we and over a dozen of our neighbors met with Daniel Gonzales of the Department of Public Works to express our concerns with the design. While Daniel acknowledged that communication “could have been better,” he said he didn’t think it was likely that he would agree to redesign the intersection. He also said that the street would be ground down and repaved “soon,” but couldn’t say when, locking in the poor design choices. There is some urgency to the matter. We are therefore asking you to instruct the Department of Public Works to develop and implement a design for the intersection that returns the sidewalk to its former level and provides safety when crossing the street for all residents. In the long run, making these changes now rather than letting them fester, will save the city money. To give you a sense of the changes, see the attached beforeand-after pictures. –Dr. Elizabeth McDonald and J High Corner of Manor Drive and Holly Place — Before. articles.text: The new school year is underway as Piedmont athletes get set to hit the fields and courts. It can be easy to forget all that transpired the previous year as coaches turn the page and look toward their new rosters. There were several moments last year that made a strong impression on this writer. In this article, the Post reflects on our favorite five events and memories from last year. 1 Boys’ Soccer’s North Coast Section championship Coach Todd Sullivan is among the most emotional coaches at the school during games, often shouting at referees and urging his players to achieve great results. Once the final whistle blew on that February 26 night at Witter Field when PHS defeated No. 2 University 1-0 for the Division 4 North Coast Section championship, Sullivan shot his hands in the air, gave me an embracing hug when congratulating him, and had his emotions on high during our postgame interview. In a rattling voice he described that he might break into tears any moment. Even a bucket of icecold Gatorade dumped on him on a cold February night brought no shivers. Instead, it produced an air of satisfaction knowing that that Piedmont had finally captured an NCS banner. 2. Boys’ Water Polo captures first league title It’s difficult to think of another person more deserving of a championship than water polo coach John Savage. Piedmont’s 12-8 win over No. 1 seeded Berkeley Staff Photos Boys’ soccer coach Todd Sullivan gets doused with Gatorade after Piedmont beat University to win the North Coast Section championship. Boys’ water polo coach John Savage pumps his fists after his team won the league championship for the first time in school history, on October 30 for the WACC title was a long time coming for the school that has churned out collegiate talent over the years. It was the team’s first league banner in 15 years. As the final whistle blew, Savage pumped his fists with clipboard in hand while his team celebrated in the pool. 3. “Daddy’s Money” game with Berkeley football 2021 was a difficult season for Piedmont football, which played a full season with a roster of only 19 varsity players and finished with a 2-7 record. But on October 8 at the Yellowjackets’ field, the Highlanders beat large-enrollment Berkeley 28-26 in a comeback. The Berkeley student section provided a hostile setting, chanting “Daddy’s money” toward Piedmont throughout. But PHS quarterback Adhi Bornstein drove the team 55 yards with 2:41 left in the game, completing the winning TD pass to receiver Ryan McConathy. Bornstein had his best game of the year with 261 yards, three touchdowns, and on defense, making an interception to seal the deal. The football team’s 28-26 win over Berkeley came in a hostile environment. Quarterback Adhi Bornstein led the team with 261 yards passing and three touchdowns. The boys’ lacrosse team captured its sixth straight WACC title in a heated 10-9 win over top-seeded Bishop O’Dowd, with new PHS coach Alex Yu defeating his former team.

articles.text: Next up: Cincinnati Masters, U.S. Open this month Photos courtesy of EuroSport Mackie McDonald recently competed in the Cincinnati Masters, making the Round of 32. Mackie McDonald is playing his way through the summer schedule in preparation for the U.S. Open later this month (August 29 to September 11). This week, McDonald reached the Round of 32 at the Cincinnati Masters tournament, nearly double-bageling Nikoloz Basilashvili 6-0, 6-1 on Sunday, August 14 but losing in straight sets to No. 3 seed Carlos Alcaraz on Tuesday, August 16, 6-3, 6-2. Against Basilashvili, McDonald recorded eight aces and won 90 percent of points on his first serve, while claiming six of 11 break point opportunities. It was a dominant win over the world’s No. 34 overall ranked player on the ATP World Tour. McDonald took three break points in the first set as the returner and another three in the second set. McDonald has played well against Basilashvili throughout his career. This marks his third career win over the Georgian. In the match with Alcaraz, the loss came against the world’s No. 4 overall ranked player and a teenage phenom at just 19 years old. Alcaraz started the first set by stealing a point as the returner, while Mackie battled to 4-3 in the first. However, the Spaniard won the final two games, including the sixth game as the returner. In the second set, the match sat at 2-2, but Alcaraz claimed four straight games to win, including two break points. Alcaraz finished with five aces and claimed four of seven break point opportunities. McDonald is now ranked No. 72 in the world after reaching a career high of No. 48 earlier this month. McDonald lost in three sets to No. 44 Emil Ruusuvouri in the Citi Open’s first round on August 2, 1-6, 6-4, 6-4. He also lost in the first round of the Canadian Open on August 8 to No. 39 Alex Molcan in a close match, 7-6 (7-1), 6-4. Looking ahead to the prestigious U.S. Open, the event in 2016 was McDonald’s Grand Slam debut, where he reached the first round. McDonald reached the second round in 2021, defeating No. 27 seed David Goffin 6-2, 7-5, 6-3 in the first round but lost to Kei Nishikori in the second round, 7-6 (7-3), 6-3, 6-7 (7-5), 2-6, 6-3. Mackie McDonald lost to No. 4 world ranked Carlos Alcaraz in the second round of the Cincinnati Masters. Mackie McDonald gears up for the next Grand Slam tournament, the U.S. Open from August 29-September 11.

articles.text: 3 points back of playoff qualification zone, 9 matches left It was another tie for Oakland Roots, this time with Detroit City, after leading 1-0. Charlie Dennis’ scored for Oakland in the 50th minute, but Detroit equalized it with three minutes left in regulation on a goal by Francis Atuahene. The result brings Oakland’s record to six wins, 12 ties, and seven losses with nine games left in the season. With 30 points, it’s shaping up to be a thick race for a final playoff spot in the Western Conference. Following the weekend’s results, the Roots are in ninthplace and two points behind eighth-place Los Dos (which has one game in hand), three back of Las Vegas (one game in hand) in the seventh-place playoff barrier, and four back of sixth-place El Paso–which has played one more match than Oakland and plays again on August 20. Behind Roots, meanwhile, is Phoenix and Monterey Bay with 29 points each. Roots dropping points is a painfully common occurrence in 2022 with Saturday’s result being the eighth time Oakland has either tied or lost from a winning position. How valuable would’ve been those 24 points? Here’s a list Charlie Dennis scored for Oakland after being in position when Detroit’s keeper misplayed a pass. It marked the eighth time they dropped points from a winning position after leading 1-0. of those games: 3-2 loss to Monterey Bay, March 26; Roots led 2-1 after 49 minutes. 2-2 tie at New Mexico United, March 30; Roots led 1-0 after eight minutes. 1-1 tie at El Paso, April 23; Roots led 1-0 after 23 minutes. 1-1 tie at Las Vegas, May 14; Roots led 1-0 after three minutes. 2-1 loss to New Mexico United, June 15; Roots led 1-0 after 20 minutes. 1-1 tie at San Antonio, June 18; Roots led 1-0 after 29 minutes. 3-3 tie at Sacramento Republic, July 9; Roots led 3-2 after 70 minutes. 1-1 tie at Detroit City, August 13; Roots led 1-0 after 50 minutes. In Saturday’s draw, Roots had its chances and had better looks before and after the 50th minute goal. Dennis nearly had an early goal in the ninth minute when his left footed shot forced a diving save. In the 18th, Darek Formella had a shot on target saved after receiving a feed by Edgardo Rito on the counter attack. Dennis’ goal in the 50th came from a disastrous ball by Detroit keeper Nate Steinwascher, which went straight to Dennis, enabling him to uncork a left-footed shot into the net. Rito perhaps had the most clear look in the 65th with an opportunity to put Oakland up 2-nil when Dennis found him with a ball over the top, but Edgardo’s left footed shot (his weaker foot) skied by the left post. In the 82nd minute, Oakland subbed in Joseph Nane for Mikael Johnsen in a defensive move. But Detroit struck just five minutes later when striker Antoine Hoppenot went down the right side with the Roots’ defense strung out of position. The DCFC striker was able to find Atuahene with acres of space in a one-on-one situation, leading to the equalizer. It was an unfortunate turn after a solid game by the defense to not allow many clear looks. Detroit finished with 10 shots, three on target, after going into halftime with three shot attempts and none on target. Oakland, finished with 12 shots, three on target, five blocked and three big opportunities missed. Roots coach Juan Guerra shared his thoughts on Twitter, voicing optimism after playing in a difficult environment at Detroit’s Keyworth Stadium. “Tonight we were able to play our way in a very tough environment. articles.text: The largest fire in 2022 is just about out of the national spotlight and near full containment at 95 percent as of Tuesday night, currently at 60,392 acres burned— gaining just three acres in size over the last week. Firefighting efforts are still focusing on unburned vegetation within the containment lines. “Firefighters continue suppression repair efforts and are patrolling throughout the fire perimeter. Crews are paying particular attention to areas of unburned vegetation within the interior of the fire containment lines, which have been producing smoke and heat. Aircraft was brought in to conduct aerial suppression operations on one of these pockets in the southwestern fire area. Three hand crews and a strike team of engines also conducted ground suppression and the “hot spot” posed no threat to the containment lines,” wrote Inciweb, a federal fire information site. Inciweb continues that only two miles of the fire is considered uncontained, while fire prevention work has contructed 204 total miles of containment lines. “Additionally, firefighters have been granted access to the McKinney Creek Road area, and repair work will begin within the next few days. As of Sunday evening, firefighters have constructed 62 miles of containment line by hand, and heavy equipment has constructed 142 miles of containment line. Only two miles of the fire is considered “uncontained” at this time. Forward progression of the fire has stopped, but steep terrain and the abundance of hazard trees are making it difficult for firefighters to perform mop-up in this area. Crews will keep working as safety allows,” wrote Inciweb. Photo courtesy of Redding.com Firefighter efforts have helped contain the McKinney Fire to 95 percent. Photo courtesy of Redding.com Fire prevention efforts have created over 200 miles of containment lines.

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California’s free events on Friday Nights will continue this fall, with food trucks, music, and art activities inspired by the museum’s current exhibitions. Beginning at 5 p.m., an assortment of food trucks on 10th street between Oakland and Fallon Streets will be parked, with beer and wine available. The variety of food changes weekly. Activities and music will be available on the museum’s outdoor lawn. Oakland-based landscape architect and MacArthur Genius award-winner Walter Hood, with architecture firm Mark Cavagnero Associates, led the project design. Kalingafornia Laga is a weaving collective of Filipino American women in the San Francisco Bay Area who preserve, promote, and maintain indigenous backstrap weaving traditions from Kalinga. Sheng Lor is a Hmong American fiber artist whose practice is motivated by a desire to connect to cultural practices of her elders, which are rooted in shamanism and land stewardship. articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse presents Follies onstage now through September 10. The musical is based on a book of the same name written by James Goldman, with music and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim. Goldman was an American playwright, novelist, and screenwriter, whose first play on Broadway was a comedy about life in the army, Blood, Sweat, and Stanley Poole (1961), written with his brother William. Other work for the stage includes A Family Affair, a collaboration with John Kander, starring Shelley Berman; Evening Primrose (1966), Oliver Twist (1982), Anna Karenina (1985), Anatasia: The Mystery of Anna (1986), and Tolstoy (1996). Goldman’s novels include The Man from Greek and Roman (1974), Myself as Witness (1980), and Fulton County (1989). Follies opened on Broadway in 1971 to critical acclaim; it was nominated for 11 Tony awards and won seven. The original production is the second-most costly production performed on Broadway to date. The play focuses on two couples, Buddy and Sally Durant Plummer and Benjamin and Phyllis Rogers Stone, who are attending the reunion of crumbling theatre in between the world wars. Sally and Phyllis were showgirls in the Follies, both in failing marriages. The cast includes Caroline Altman, Catrina Manahan, Samantha Rose Cárdenas, Ann Warque, Danielle Cheiken, Emily Corbo, Rene Collins, Chachi Delgado, M.Javi Harnly, and Catrina Manahan. articles.text: There are thousands of stories out there. Columnists such as Herb Caen and Dwight Chapin engaged the readers’ interest every day. So did radio broadcaster Paul Harvey. Yes, everyone has a story. One of the most interesting stories in the history of music involves the duo of operetta composers W. S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan. A more interesting duo probably never existed. Another story of particular interest is the San Francisco-based Lamplighters Music Theater. They have been presenting Gilbert and Sullivan productions for 70 years. That’s quite a run. I took the opportunity to attend the Sunday performance of their most recent production, Iolanthe, in the Yerba Buena Center in San Francisco. The production was everything you would expect from the Lamplighters…The costumes were colorful, and the production was lively. The orchestra played with precision. Overall, the staging was excellent. My only criticism is that the diction was sometimes not as clear as it might have been. But when I moved to the second row, it seemed to improve. Gilbert and Sullivan knew how to thumb their nose at almost everybody in society and positions of authority. They also knew how to do it in such a way that the object of their humor did not respond with anger – something requiring extraordinary talent and skill. Iolanthe is a typical example of political satire. It’s kind of like the joke where someone asks someone in a high position if it is possible to be both ignorant and apathetic. The “self important person“ answers: I don’t know and I don’t care. Gilbert and Sullivan use this routine frequently. Iolanthe pokes fun at just about everybody. There was absolutely no doubt that English Prime Minister William Gladstone was the object of much of this barbed humor and perhaps surprisingly was delighted with what Gilbert and Sullivan had created. Sadly, times have changed. Many people in high places now can’t take a joke. . There is one final performance of Iolanthe next weekend in Livermore. I gibe it my highest recommendations. And now the food part When I first moved to San Francisco, you could find good dim sum in almost any restaurant. I usually went with Chinese friends and always had a good time. Over time, however, It became more difficult to find good dim sum. That changed last week when I went to the Saigon Seafood Harbor Restaurant on Pierce Street in Richmond. In the old days waitresses and waiters used to come around with carts and you’d pick what you want. This dim sum restaurant has menus, and, more importantly, has great food. I never had better roast duck. Everything on our gigantic banquet was superb. Another recent discovery was Pomella restaurant located at 3770 Piedmont Avenue. This is a popular Middle Eastern restaurant. Everything that my party ordered was delectable. If you park in the adjacent lot, please note that the meters are enforced until midnight. I didn’t read the small print… And I mean SMALL print… The parking fine is $30. Next week we might look at how opera uses revisionist history. Forget the Barber of Seville. Forget the Spanish background of Carmen. And as for Aida…forget about Egypt. Put on your thinking caps and study your geography. And then forget everything. Operetta composers Gilbert & Sullivan.

articles.text: Quinton Aaron and Sandra Bullock in The Blind Side Review by Chris Honoré The trailer for The Blind Side, released in 2009, has the appearance of another slick Hollywood happy meal. The film will be a two-hour sports cliché, the audience leaving the theater feeling somewhat satisfied but also a bit empty. Instead, surprisingly, the movie proves to be a solid drama, with Sandra Bullock as can-do southern belle, Leigh Anne Tuohy, giving her best performance in years and redeeming herself after the disastrous All About Steve. The true story, based on the book by Michael Lewis, while blatantly sentimental, tells the appealing story of Michael Oher (Quinton Aaron), aka Big Mike, a homeless black teen from the projects (ironically named Hurt Village), who is enrolled in a private Christian school in Memphis, Tennessee. Late one wintry night he is spotted by Leigh Anne and her husband, Sean (Tim McGraw), walking on a busy road. It’s bitterly cold and Michael admits that he has nowhere to go. They take him home, thus beginning the transformation of Michael from an undereducated, silent mountain of a kid to a star athlete who is eventually drafted by the Baltimore Ravens. It’s a remarkable journey, tempered to be sure by Michael’s stoic silence and his reluctance to trust, at least initially, this most improbable family that has taken him into their hearts. But he learns. And in the process begins a completely new life. Is the feel-good ending telegraphed almost from the first frame? Of course. But no matter. The Blind Side is a sweet movie. The Blind Side. Directed by John Lee Hancock. Starring Sandra Bullock, Tim McGraw, Quinton Aaron, and Kathy Bates. 2 hrs., 8 min. Rated PG-13. Released in theaters in 2009; reviewed then in the Post. articles.text: Madagascar is filled with gags, risky escapes, Looney Toon moments, and, of course, some standard life lessons (the importance of friendship, and be careful what you wish for). The story is likely best suited for older kids and tweens. The narrative is set in the New York Zoo, at least that’s where the adventure begins. Marty the zebra (Chris Rock) is celebrating his 10th birthday and rather than feeling cheerful, he is cranky, bored with the zoo’s day-in and day-out routine. His best bud, Alex the lion (Ben Stiller), a zoo favorite, tries to cheer him up, but to no avail. Alex loves to perform for the visitors, as well as enjoying his daily diet of raw steaks. One day Marty, still moping around, hears that there’s a scheme in the works by the crafty penguins, Skipper (Tom McGrath), Kowalski (Chris Miller), Rico (Jeff Katzenberg), and Private (Chris Knight). But it turns out the group is planning an escape. Naturally, Marty is inspired. It seems the penguin cohort wants to take over a ship and head toward colder climes. Marty convinces his friends, Gloria, the sassy hippo (Jada Pinkett Smith), Melman the giraffe (David Schwimmer), and Alex to join him in the break out. But things don’t go quite as planned, and the foursome end up stranded on the sandy shores of Madagascar, a jungle island island off the coast of Africa. They soon discover that there’s a colony of lemurs living there, led by King Julian (Sasha Baron Cohen). They also discover that they are now in the middle of the wild, exactly the place Marty had dreamed of. But what the gang soon learns is that perhaps the zoo is not all that bad. The wild jungles of the island are not all that userfriendly, and from Alex’s point of view, those ready-to-eat steaks are nowhere to be found. Soon he starts to eye Marty’s haunch as hunger sets in. All he wants is a nibble. Luckily, the penguins find a way to feed Alex some sushi. Soon Marty begins to wonder about how they might return to the zoo. It’s not as boring as he thought and being pampered was not all that bad. All of this is silly, funny, frisky storytelling that begins from the minute that they arrive on the island. Madagascar. Dreamworks animation. Directed by Eric Darnell & Tom McGrath. With voices of Ben Stiller, Chris Rock, and David Schwimmer. 1 hr., 26 min. Rated PG. Released in 2005. Now Streaming on Vudu/ Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: Madagascar a silly adventure from NYC to Africa

articles.text: Perhaps part of the appeal of Buck is that from the first frame of this fine documentary Buck Brannaman is the quintessential cowboy, an iconic image that has resonated for generations. Buck travels the U.S., conducting horse clinics for owners who have young colts who need breaking in, or horses that are a bit dysfunctional. So Buck shares his approach, one that is firm and gentle and always respectful of the horse. He guides, cajoles and reassures, taking a skittish animal and transforming it. Think of his methods as Zen and the art of horse handling. The film also includes Buck’s tragic backstory. As youngsters, he and his brother were taken from state to state as trick ropers. When they weren’t performing at rodeos and fairgrounds, their father physically abused them, leaving them scarred. Buck is testimony to how one man, with grace and will and discipline, altered every aspect of his life. When young, he was simply looking to find a peaceful place where he didn’t feel threatened. What he found instead was his life’s work. To come even briefly to know this man is to understand how elusive it is to do what you love and feel complete. To know that your insights, your knowledge, created out of years of experience, are significant and offer a certain wisdom regarding the human condition. Buck tells people firmly that horses mirror their owners, and how people treat their horses is how they treat others – family, friends and strangers. Buck is a remarkable film. Buck. Directed by Cindy Meehi. With Buck Brannaman, Gary Meyers, Bib Frazier. Documentary. 1 hr., 28 min. Released in 2011. Now streaming on Prime/ Apple tv. Buck Brannaman stars as himself in the documentary Buck.

Madagascar a silly adventure from NYC to Africa By Chris Honoré Madagascar is filled with gags, risky escapes, Looney Toon moments, and, of course, some standard life lessons (the importance of friendship, and be careful what you wish for). The story is likely best suited for older kids and tweens. The narrative is set in the New York Zoo, at least that’s where the adventure begins. Marty the zebra (Chris Rock) is celebrating his 10th birthday and rather than feeling cheerful, he is cranky, bored with the zoo’s day-in and day-out routine. His best bud, Alex the lion (Ben Stiller), a zoo favorite, tries to cheer him up, but to no avail. Alex loves to perform for the visitors, as well as enjoying his daily diet of raw steaks. One day Marty, still moping around, hears that there’s a scheme in the works by the crafty penguins, Skipper (Tom McGrath), Kowalski (Chris Miller), Rico (Jeff Katzenberg), and Private (Chris Knight). Marty convinces his friends, Gloria, the sassy hippo (Jada Pinkett Smith), Melman the giraffe (David Schwimmer), and Alex to join him in the break out. But things don’t go quite as planned, and the foursome end up stranded on the sandy shores of Madagascar, a jungle island island off the coast of Africa. They soon discover that there’s a colony of lemurs living there, led by King Julian (Sasha Baron Cohen). They also discover that they are now in the middle of the wild, exactly the place Marty had dreamed of. But what the gang soon learns is that perhaps the zoo is not all that bad. All he wants is a nibble. Luckily, the penguins find a way to feed Alex some sushi. Soon Marty begins to wonder about how they might return to the zoo. Buck – a remarkable story Perhaps part of the appeal of Buck is that from the first frame of this fine documentary Buck Brannaman is the quintessential cowboy, an iconic image that has resonated for generations. Buck travels the U.S., conducting horse clinics for owners who have young colts who need breaking in, or horses that are a bit dysfunctional. So Buck shares his approach, one that is firm and gentle and always respectful of the horse. He guides, cajoles and reassures, taking a skittish animal and transforming it. Think of his methods as Zen and the art of horse handling. The film also includes Buck’s tragic backstory. As youngsters, he and his brother were taken from state to state as trick ropers. When they weren’t performing at rodeos and fairgrounds, their father physically abused them, leaving them scarred. Buck is testimony to how one man, with grace and will and discipline, altered every aspect of his life. When young, he was simply looking to find a peaceful place where he didn’t feel threatened. What he found instead was his life’s work. To come even briefly to know this man is to understand how elusive it is to do what you love and feel complete. To know that your insights, your knowledge, created out of years of experience, are significant and offer a certain wisdom regarding the human condition. Buck tells people firmly that horses mirror their owners, and how people treat their horses is how they treat others – family, friends and strangers. Buck is a remarkable film. Buck. articles.text: If you’re like most people, your work has been a central part of your life. So, wouldn’t it be nice to have the flexibility to decide when you no longer want to work? Many people of retirement age have achieved this type of control. In fact, two-thirds of workers ages 65 and older say they work primarily because they want to, not because they have to, according to a 2021 study by Edward Jones and Age Wave. But that means that one-third of workers in this age group feel financially compelled to work. This doesn’t necessarily mean they dislike the work they do — but it’s probably fair to say they would have liked the option of not working. How can you give yourself this choice? You can start by asking yourself these questions: • When do I want to retire? You’ll want to identify the age at which you wish to retire. You may change your mind later and move this date up or back, but it’s a good idea to have a target in mind. • What sort of retirement lifestyle do I want? When you retire, do you anticipate staying close to home and pursuing your hobbies, or do you hope to travel the world? Would you like to spend your time volunteering? Open your own business or do some consulting? Clearly, some of these choices will require more resources than others, so you’ll want to follow a financial strategy that aligns with the retirement lifestyle you intend to pursue. • Am I saving and investing enough? As you chart your course toward your retirement journey, you’ll want to assess the sources of income you’ll have available. If you think you may be falling short of achieving your retirement goals, you may need to consider saving more. • When should I start taking Social Security? articles.text: It was relatively quiet at the Exedra last Wednesday morning at 10:30 as the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group assembled for their weekly walk. Two hours earlier the frenzied, first-day-ofschool rush had just gone on at the Exedra. On another lovely morning, a strong turnout of 31 walkers and two K-9 best friends were ready to walk. The group decided to go to some “roads not taken” streets, inspired by Dave DeRoche and his baritone voice reading Robert Frost’s “The Road Not Taken” to the group. This poem ends with, “Two roads diverged in a wood, and I – I took the one less traveled by, and that has made all the difference.” It was noted that one of the great things about Walking on Wednesdays is that the group can take a less traveled Piedmont road one week, and then take the more traveled one the next Wednesday. The group headed for Bellevue Avenue by way of blocklong Sierra Avenue. They stopped to talk about two Julia Morgan designed homes that architect Will Adams had described on a tour he led last year. Turning onto Sheridan, they went to Caperton Avenue, then traveled Richardson Way and onto Lakeview Avenue, and the little-known Poplar Way, ending at Mountain Avenue near the intersection with Bellevue Avenue. The corner is marked by an historic redwood tree, site of the city’s first tree lighting ceremony. At the far end of Bellevue they came to a beautiful, large home with a long driveway, a majestic oak tree in the front year and a great view of San Francisco. The group continued on to Pacific and Hagar Avenues, enjoying fabulous, clear views of San Francisco along the way. On Bell Avenue, at the top of Piedmont, there were more great views. From Bell the group began its descent on Scenic Avenue to Alta Avenue and then down a 163-foot set of steep stairs to the lower portion of Scenic. On Scenic they saw the house inhabited around 1900 by artist Xavier Martínez, a well-known bohemian figure in San Francisco and the East Bay. This section of Piedmont was a bit of an artist colony during the turn of the century. It was then an easy return to the center of town via Blair, Pacific, Mountain, and Highland Avenues. It had been a two-mile walk in 90 minutes with beautiful homes and views enjoyed along many not-often-taken roads. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Participants on the Walking on Wednesday outing on August 10 included Marion Lim Yankowitz, Sarah Johnson, Nadine Guffanti, Elizabeth Richter, Jim Kellogg, Pat Keller, Karin Fetherston with K-9 best friend Vivie, Alan Goldhammer, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Brenda Ferrero, Renee Goldhammer, Bob Wong, Kat Lang, Harriette Louie, Phil Witte, Melba Yee, Charlene Louie, Gloria DaSilva, Priscilla Wanerus, Dick Carter, Stella Houston, Sherry Jacobs, Pat Sheehan, Albert Chen, Dave DeRoche, and Meghan Bennett. The group was happy to have Nancy Olsen and Larry Olsen back for their first post-pandemic walks; as well as Siow Fang Tan and Christine Calliste now that their summer vacations are over.
